cmo-cmo-2008-01.title: Areas and a midline
cmo-cmo-2008-01.body:
Write $[\cdot]$ for area. Since $CM$ halves the quadrilateral, $[AMCD] = [ABCD] - [MBC] = \frac12[ABCD]$; since $AN$ halves it, $[ANCD] = [ABCD] - [ABN] = \frac12[ABCD]$. By convexity, $M$ and $N$ lie on the same side of the diagonal $AC$ as $B$, and $D$ on the other side, so $[AMCD] = [AMC] + [ACD]$ and $[ANCD] = [ANC] + [ACD]$. Hence $[AMC] = [ANC]$: the triangles on the common base $AC$ have equal heights, with $M$, $N$ on the same side of $AC$, so $MN \parallel AC$.

Let $m$ be the line through $D$ parallel to $AC$. As $D$ is on the other side of $AC$ from $B$, the ray $BA$ extended beyond $A$ meets $m$ at a point $P$, and the ray $BC$ extended beyond $C$ meets $m$ at a point $Q$; and $D$ lies on segment $PQ$ (it lies inside angle $ABC$).

Now $A$ lies between $M$ and $P$ on line $AB$, so
$$[MPC] = [MAC] + [APC] = [MAC] + [ADC] = [AMCD] = \tfrac12[ABCD] = [MBC],$$
where $[APC] = [ADC]$ because $P$ and $D$ are on the line $m \parallel AC$ (equal heights over base $AC$). Triangles $MPC$ and $MBC$ have the same apex $C$ and bases $MP$, $BM$ on the same line, so $MP = BM$: $M$ is the midpoint of $BP$. In the same way $[NQA] = [NCA] + [CQA] = [NCA] + [CDA] = [ANCD] = [ABN]$, so $NQ = BN$ and $N$ is the midpoint of $BQ$.

So $MN$ is the midline of triangle $BPQ$ parallel to $PQ$. The homothety with centre $B$ and ratio $\frac12$ maps segment $PQ$ onto segment $MN$, and maps $D \in PQ$ to the midpoint of $BD$. Hence the midpoint of $BD$ lies on segment $MN$, i.e. $MN$ bisects $BD$. ∎

(The hypothesis that $AB$ is the longest side is not needed for this argument; it only guarantees that suitable $M$ and $N$ exist on the sides.)

cmo-cmo-2008-02.title: Involution, then additivity
cmo-cmo-2008-02.body:
Both $f(x) = x$ and $f(x) = -x$ work: $f(2x + y) = 2x + y$, respectively $f(-2x - y) = 2x + y$. We show there are no others.

**$f(0) = 0$.** Putting $y = x$ gives $f(3f(x)) = 3x$ for all $x$. Replacing $x$ by $3f(x)$ there: $f\big(3f(3f(x))\big) = 3\cdot 3f(x)$, and since $f(3f(x)) = 3x$, this is $f(9x) = 9f(x)$. At $x = 0$: $f(0) = 9f(0)$, so $f(0) = 0$.

**$f$ is an involution.** With $x = 0$: $f(f(y)) = y$ for all $y$. In particular $f$ is a bijection.

**$f$ is additive.** Apply $f$ to both sides of the equation and use $f(f(z)) = z$:
$$2f(x) + f(y) = f(2x + y) \quad \text{for all } x, y.$$
With $y = 0$: $2f(x) = f(2x)$. Hence $f(2x) + f(y) = f(2x + y)$; as $2x$ ranges over all rationals, $f(u + v) = f(u) + f(v)$ for all rationals $u, v$.

**$f$ is linear.** From additivity, $f(0) = 0$, $f(-u) = -f(u)$ and, by induction, $f(nu) = nf(u)$ for integers $n$. Let $k = f(1)$. For integers $p$ and $q \ge 1$: $q\,f(p/q) = f(p) = pk$, so $f(p/q) = kp/q$. Thus $f(x) = kx$ for all rational $x$.

Finally $f(f(x)) = k^2x = x$ forces $k^2 = 1$, so $f(x) = x$ or $f(x) = -x$. ∎

cmo-cmo-2008-02.title: A different substitution
cmo-cmo-2008-02.body:
Put $x = y = 2f(z) + f(w)$ in the equation. Then $f(x) = f(y) = 2z + w$ by the equation itself, and the left side becomes $f(3(2z + w))$:
$$f(6z + 3w) = 3\,(2f(z) + f(w)) = 6f(z) + 3f(w) \quad \text{for all } z, w.$$
With $z = w = 0$: $f(0) = 9f(0)$, so $f(0) = 0$. With $w = 0$: $f(6z) = 6f(z)$; with $z = 0$: $f(3w) = 3f(w)$. Hence $f(6z + 3w) = f(6z) + f(3w)$, and writing $u = 6z$, $v = 3w$ (arbitrary rationals), $f(u + v) = f(u) + f(v)$. As in the first solution, $f(x) = kx$ with $k = f(1)$. Substituting $x = y = 1$ into the original equation: $f(3k) = 3k^2 = 3$, so $k = \pm 1$. Both $f(x) = x$ and $f(x) = -x$ satisfy the equation. ∎

cmo-cmo-2008-03.title: Factor the denominators
cmo-cmo-2008-03.body:
Because $a + b + c = 1$,
$$a + bc = a(a + b + c) + bc = (a + b)(a + c),$$
and similarly $b + ca = (b+a)(b+c)$, $c + ab = (c+a)(c+b)$. Hence
$$\frac{a - bc}{a + bc} = 1 - \frac{2bc}{(a+b)(a+c)},$$
and with $\Pi = (a+b)(b+c)(c+a)$ the left side is
$$3 - \frac{2\big(bc(b+c) + ca(c+a) + ab(a+b)\big)}{\Pi}.$$
Expanding, $\Pi = bc(b+c) + ca(c+a) + ab(a+b) + 2abc$, so the bracket equals $\Pi - 2abc$ and the left side equals
$$3 - 2 + \frac{4abc}{\Pi} = 1 + \frac{4abc}{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}.$$
By AM-GM, $a + b \ge 2\sqrt{ab}$, $b + c \ge 2\sqrt{bc}$, $c + a \ge 2\sqrt{ca}$, so $\Pi \ge 8abc$ and the left side is at most $1 + \frac12 = \frac32$. Equality holds exactly when $a = b = c = \frac13$. ∎

cmo-cmo-2008-03.title: Reduce to the harmonic–arithmetic mean inequality
cmo-cmo-2008-03.body:
As in the first solution, the left side equals $1 + \frac{4abc}{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}$. Using $a + b = 1 - c$ etc.,
$$(a+b)(b+c)(c+a) = (1-a)(1-b)(1-c) = 1 - (a+b+c) + (ab+bc+ca) - abc = (ab + bc + ca) - abc.$$
So the inequality is equivalent to $\frac{4abc}{(ab+bc+ca) - abc} \le \frac12$, i.e.
$$ab + bc + ca \ge 9abc \iff \frac1a + \frac1b + \frac1c \ge 9 = \frac{9}{a+b+c}.$$
The last inequality is $(a + b + c)\left(\frac1a + \frac1b + \frac1c\right) \ge 9$, which is the Cauchy–Schwarz (or HM–AM) inequality. ∎

cmo-cmo-2008-04.title: Primes with f(p) = p
cmo-cmo-2008-04.body:
**$f(p) \in \{1, p\}$.** Taking $n = p$: $f(p)^p \equiv p \pmod{f(p)}$, and the left side is $\equiv 0$, so $f(p) \mid p$, i.e. $f(p) = 1$ or $f(p) = p$.

Let $S$ be the set of primes $p$ with $f(p) = p$. For $p \in S$ the condition says $f(n)^p \equiv n \pmod p$, and by Fermat $f(n)^p \equiv f(n)$, so it says $f(n) \equiv n \pmod p$. For $p \notin S$ the condition is modulo $1$, hence always true. So **$f$ is a solution iff $f(p) \in \{1, p\}$ for all primes $p$, and $f(n) \equiv n \pmod p$ for all $n$ and all $p \in S$** (where $S$ is defined by $f$).

**$S$ infinite.** Then $f(n) - n$ is divisible by infinitely many primes, so $f(n) = n$ for every $n$. And $f(n) = n$ is a solution ($n^p \equiv n \pmod p$ by Fermat).

**$S$ empty.** Then $f(p) = 1$ for every prime and the condition is vacuous: every such $f$ (with arbitrary values at non-primes) is a solution.

**$S$ finite and nonempty.** Let $q$ be the largest prime in $S$. Every prime $p > q$ has $f(p) = 1$, and the condition for the prime $q$ with $n = p$ gives $1 = f(p)^q \equiv p \pmod q$. Suppose $q \ge 3$. Let $Q$ be the product of all odd primes up to $q$. Then $Q + 2$ is odd and is $\equiv 2 \pmod{p'}$ for each odd prime $p' \le q$, so all its prime factors exceed $q$, hence are $\equiv 1 \pmod q$, and so $Q + 2 \equiv 1 \pmod q$. But $q \mid Q$, so $Q + 2 \equiv 2 \pmod q$, and $2 \not\equiv 1$ since $q \ge 3$. Contradiction. Hence $q = 2$ and $S = \{2\}$: $f(2) = 2$, $f(p) = 1$ for every odd prime $p$, and the condition reduces to $f(n) \equiv n \pmod 2$ for all $n$ (consistent with $f(2) = 2$ and $f(p) = 1$ for odd $p$). Every such function is a solution.

**Answer:** $f(n) = n$ for all $n$; or any $f$ with $f(p) = 1$ for all primes $p$; or any $f$ with $f(2) = 2$, $f(p) = 1$ for all odd primes $p$, and $f(n)$ of the same parity as $n$ for all $n$. ∎

cmo-cmo-2008-05.title: Classify by the first moves
cmo-cmo-2008-05.body:
A rook walk is determined by the sequence of squares it visits, so we count self-avoiding paths of unit steps between edge-adjacent squares. Let $r_n = R(3, n)$ and denote by $(i, j)$ the square in row $i$ from the bottom and column $j$ from the left; walks go from $(1,1)$ to $(3,1)$. We have $r_1 = 1$.

Let $n \ge 2$. Every walk is of exactly one of these kinds.

1. *The walk $(1,1) \to (2,1) \to (3,1)$:* $1$ walk.
2. *Walks avoiding $(2,1)$.* They must start $(1,1) \to (1,2)$ and end $(3,2) \to (3,1)$, and in between form a walk from $(1,2)$ to $(3,2)$ on columns $2, \ldots, n$: $r_{n-1}$ walks.
3. *Walks through $(2,1)$, other than kind 1.* The square $(2,1)$ has neighbours $(1,1)$, $(3,1)$, $(2,2)$. If the walk visits $(2,1)$ second, it continues to $(2,2)$ (it isn't kind 1); otherwise $(2,1)$ is entered from $(2,2)$ and left to $(3,1)$, i.e. it is the second-to-last square. Both cannot happen (the walk would be kind 1). Reflecting the board top-to-bottom and reversing the walk swaps these two sub-kinds, so they are equinumerous. Count walks starting $(1,1) \to (2,1) \to (2,2)$:

   The walk runs right along row $2$ to some $(2,k)$, $k \ge 2$, and then turns up or down (it can't return left).
   - *Up to $(3,k)$.* Row $2$ is used up to column $k$, so the squares $(3,1), \ldots, (3,k-1)$ can only be reached through $(3,k)$. Hence the walk must go straight left: $(3,k) \to \cdots \to (3,1)$. One walk for each $k = 2, \ldots, n$: $n - 1$ walks.
   - *Down to $(1,k)$.* Going left along row $1$ leads into the dead end $(1,2), \ldots, (1,k-1)$, so the walk goes right to $(1, k+1)$ (needs $k \le n-1$). Now the squares $(3,1), \ldots, (3,k)$ can only be entered from $(3, k+1)$, and once entered the walk must run straight to $(3,1)$. So the walk is: the fixed start, then a walk from $(1,k+1)$ to $(3,k+1)$ inside columns $k+1, \ldots, n$, then $(3,k) \to \cdots \to (3,1)$. That gives $r_{n-k}$ walks for each $k = 2, \ldots, n-1$.

   So this sub-kind has $(n - 1) + r_1 + r_2 + \cdots + r_{n-2}$ walks.

Therefore, for $n \ge 2$,
$$r_n = 1 + r_{n-1} + 2\big[(n-1) + r_1 + \cdots + r_{n-2}\big].$$
This gives $r_2 = 1 + 1 + 2 = 4$ and $r_3 = 1 + 4 + 2(2 + 1) = 11$, as stated. Subtracting the formula for $n$ from that for $n + 1$ ($n \ge 2$):
$$r_{n+1} - r_n = r_n - r_{n-1} + 2 + 2r_{n-1} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r_{n+1} = 2r_n + r_{n-1} + 2.$$
With $s_n = r_n + 1$ this is $s_{n+1} = 2s_n + s_{n-1}$, and it also holds for $n = 1$ if we set $r_0 = 0$ ($s_2 = 5 = 2\cdot 2 + 1$). The characteristic roots are $1 \pm \sqrt2$, and the solution with $s_0 = 1$, $s_1 = 2$ is
$$s_n = \frac{(1+\sqrt2)^{n+1} - (1-\sqrt2)^{n+1}}{2\sqrt2}$$
(check: $n = 0$ gives $1$; $n = 1$ gives $\frac{(3 + 2\sqrt2) - (3 - 2\sqrt2)}{2\sqrt2} = 2$). Hence
$$R(3, n) = \frac{(1+\sqrt2)^{n+1} - (1-\sqrt2)^{n+1}}{2\sqrt2} - 1.$$
Values: $1, 4, 11, 28, 69, 168, 407, \ldots$; a computer enumeration of all self-avoiding paths agrees for $n \le 7$.

**Answer:** $R(3,n) = \dfrac{(1+\sqrt2)^{n+1} - (1-\sqrt2)^{n+1}}{2\sqrt2} - 1$.

cmo-cmo-2008-05.title: Check with a transfer recurrence
cmo-cmo-2008-05.body:
Use the notation of the first solution. Let $S(n)$ be the set of walks whose rightmost column is column $n$; then $R(3, n) = |S(1)| + \cdots + |S(n)|$, since a walk on the $3 \times n$ board has some rightmost column $j \le n$ and is then a walk on the $3 \times j$ board reaching column $j$.

Split $S(n)$ by how the walk uses column $n$ (it enters and leaves column $n$ through column $n - 1$, and is self-avoiding): type $S_1$: the walk passes through column $n$ using exactly $(2, n)$ and $(3, n)$; type $S_2$: it uses all of $(1,n)$, $(2,n)$, $(3,n)$; type $S_3$: it uses exactly $(1,n)$ and $(2,n)$. (A walk with a single square in its last column would have to enter and leave that square from the same neighbour, impossible — except for $n = 1$, which is type $S_2$.) Let $s_i(n)$ be the sizes; $s_1(1) = s_3(1) = 0$, $s_2(1) = 1$, and $s_1 = s_3$ by top–bottom symmetry.

Every walk in $S(n+1)$ comes from a unique walk in $S(n)$ by "pushing" its column-$n$ part one column to the right, and one checks that this gives
$$s_1(n+1) = s_1(n) + s_2(n), \qquad s_2(n+1) = s_1(n) + s_2(n) + s_3(n) = 2s_1(n) + s_2(n).$$
So both $s_1$ and $s_2$ satisfy $x_{n+1} = 2x_n + x_{n-1}$, with $s_1 = 0, 1, 2, 5, 12, \ldots$ and $s_2 = 1, 1, 3, 7, 17, \ldots$, i.e.
$$s_1(n) = \frac{(1+\sqrt2)^{n-1} - (1-\sqrt2)^{n-1}}{2\sqrt2}, \qquad s_2(n) = \frac{(1+\sqrt2)^{n-1} + (1-\sqrt2)^{n-1}}{2}.$$
Summing $|S(j)| = s_2(j) + 2s_1(j)$ over $j = 1, \ldots, n$ (geometric series) gives the same formula as the first solution:
$$R(3, n) = \frac{(1+\sqrt2)^{n+1} - (1-\sqrt2)^{n+1}}{2\sqrt2} - 1.$$
(For example $n = 3$: $|S(1)| + |S(2)| + |S(3)| = 1 + 3 + 7 = 11$.)
